M: Good morning, Coastline Homestay Services, this is Greg speaking. How can I help?

M: Of course. I'll just take a few details. Can I have your full name?
W: Yes, it's Maya Prasetyo.
M: Could you spell your surname for me?
W: Sure. P-R-A-S-E-T-Y-O.
M: Thank you. And when are you planning to arrive?
W: My flight lands on the twelfth of February, but I'm staying with a friend for two nights first, so I'd like the homestay to start on the fourteenth.
M: The fourteenth of February, no problem. What will you be studying?
W: I'm starting a Bachelor of Nursing at the university near the city.

sets.transcript:
M: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to Riverbend Community Library. My name is Paul and I'm going to give you a quick introduction before you explore the building.
First, opening hours. From Monday to Friday we're open from nine in the morning until eight in the evening. A lot of people assume we keep the same hours at weekends, but on Saturdays and Sundays we open at ten and close at four.
Now, borrowing. When you first join, you can borrow up to ten items at a time. That includes books, DVDs and magazines. After you've been a member for three months, the limit goes up to fifteen.
We no longer charge fines for late returns, which surprises some people. However, if an item is more than two weeks overdue, your borrowing is suspended until you bring it back. So please do keep an eye on your due dates. You'll get an email reminder three days before.
Lots of you have asked about wi-fi. The network is free, and the password changes every month. It isn't printed on your library card, and the front desk staff are often busy, so we've put it on the posters next to the lifts on every floor.
We also have six study rooms for groups. These are very popular in exam season. You can't book them by phone any more, and you can't just turn up and take one; you need to book through our website, up to a week in advance.
Let me now tell you where things are. On the ground floor, as you came in, you'll have seen the returns desk on your left. Further along, at the back of the ground floor, is the children's section, which has its own story-time area.
If you go up to the first floor, you'll find our café, and next to it the newspapers and magazines, so you can read with a coffee. Many people expect the computer lab to be there too, but in fact it's on the third floor, along with the printing and scanning machines.
Finally, the second floor is our silent study area. Phones must be switched to silent, and no group work is allowed there. Right, let's start the tour.

sets.transcript:
W: Hello and thanks for joining today's guided walk. I'm Rachel from Seacliff Parks. Before we set off, let me tell you about the Seacliff Coastal Walk.
The full walk from Seacliff Beach to Little Bay is about six kilometres. Some guidebooks say eight, but that includes the return to the car park, which most people do by bus. It takes around two and a half hours at an easy pace.
People often ask when the best time to do the walk is. In summer, midday is far too hot and there's very little shade. Late afternoon can be nice, but the path gets crowded. Our advice is to start early in the morning, when it's cool and you'll often see dolphins.
Swimming. Little Bay has a beautiful beach, and lifeguards patrol it in summer. Swimming is allowed, but only between the red and yellow flags. The currents outside the flags are dangerous.
Dogs are welcome on the walk, but only on a lead and only before nine a.m. After that the path is too busy.
Now some practical tips. There are no shops for the first four kilometres, so please bring plenty of water. Sunscreen and a hat are also essential.
About halfway, you'll reach Gull Point Lookout. It's a great place for photos, but it's best known for whale watching. Between June and October you can see humpback whales passing on their migration.
At Little Bay there's a small café. It opens at eight and closes at three p.m., so if you're walking in the afternoon, don't count on lunch there.
Toilets are available at the start and next to the car park at Little Bay. There aren't any along the cliffs.
For safety, the cliff section of the path is closed during heavy rain, because the rocks become slippery. Check the park website before you come.
Finally, to get back, catch the number three eight zero bus from Little Bay. It runs every twenty minutes back to the city and stops at Seacliff Beach on the way. OK, let's go.

Please register your bicycle with us. It only takes five minutes and it's free, and it helps us return stolen bikes to their owners.
Lost property is kept at the security office for one month. After that, items are donated to charity.

sets.transcript:
L: Today we're looking at desalination, the process of removing salt from seawater so that it can be used for drinking and farming.
The oldest method is thermal distillation. It copies the natural water cycle: seawater is heated, the steam rises and leaves the salt behind, and then the steam is cooled and collected as fresh water. It works, but it needs huge amounts of heat.
Most modern plants use reverse osmosis instead. Here, seawater is pushed at high pressure through a membrane, a very thin sheet with tiny holes that let water molecules through but block salt.
Whichever method is used, the main cost of running a plant is energy. Building the plant is expensive, but over its life, electricity is the biggest bill.
Australia became interested in desalination during the long droughts of the early two-thousands. The country's first large plant opened in Perth in two thousand and six, and Perth now gets a significant share of its drinking water from the sea.
However, there are environmental concerns. For every litre of fresh water produced, roughly one and a half litres of waste is created. This waste, called brine, is about twice as salty as seawater.
If brine is simply poured back into the ocean, it sinks to the sea floor and can harm marine life near the outlet, especially creatures that cannot move away.
To reduce this, engineers use diffusers: pipes with many small openings that spread the brine over a wide area, so its concentration falls quickly.
Another response to criticism has been to power plants with renewable energy. Several Australian plants buy electricity from wind farms to offset their energy use.
Looking ahead, researchers are testing filters made of graphene, a material one atom thick, which could let water through with far less pressure and therefore less energy.

sets.transcript:
L: In this lecture I want to talk about bees and why they matter so much for agriculture.
Around one third of the food we eat depends, at least partly, on pollination, the transfer of pollen from one flower to another, which allows plants to produce fruit and seeds.
In Australia, the European honeybee is the best-known pollinator, but it isn't native. Honeybees were brought to the colony in eighteen twenty-two, mainly for honey.
Australia also has around two thousand native bee species. Most of them are solitary: rather than living in large hives, each female builds her own small nest.
Some native bees are better pollinators than honeybees for certain crops. The blue-banded bee, for example, uses buzz pollination, vibrating its body to shake pollen loose. This is particularly effective for tomatoes, which honeybees cannot pollinate well.
What threatens bees? Disease and climate change play a role, but the main threat is the loss of habitat, as bushland is cleared for housing and large farms.
Certain pesticides are also a concern. Even in small doses they can affect a bee's sense of direction, so it cannot find its way back to the nest.
Farmers are responding in several ways. Many now plant strips of wildflowers between fields, which provide food for bees when crops are not flowering.
Pollination is also a business. Almond growers rent hundreds of thousands of hives each spring, when the trees flower, and beekeepers move their hives by truck from farm to farm.
This system came under pressure in twenty twenty-two, when the varroa mite, a parasite that has destroyed hives overseas, was detected in New South Wales.
Finally, ordinary people can help researchers. A free app allows anyone to photograph bees and record sightings, building a map of where different species live.

sets.title: Part 4 · Lecture: the history of tea
sets.transcript:
L: Today's lecture is about the history of tea, one of the most widely consumed drinks in the world after water.
Tea comes from the leaves of a single plant, Camellia sinensis. Green, black and oolong tea all come from the same plant; the difference lies in how the leaves are processed, especially how long they are exposed to air, which is called oxidation.
Tea was first drunk in China, probably as a medicine. By the eighth century, it had become a popular everyday drink, and a scholar called Lu Yu wrote the first book entirely about tea.
Tea reached Europe in the early seventeenth century, brought by Dutch traders. At first it was very expensive and drunk mainly by the wealthy. In Britain, high taxes led to widespread smuggling until the tax was greatly reduced in 1784.
In the nineteenth century, the British began growing tea in India, partly to reduce their dependence on China. Large plantations were established in Assam and later in Darjeeling, and India eventually became one of the world's largest producers.
Today, the biggest producer is China, followed by India and Kenya. Interestingly, the country that drinks the most tea per person is not in Asia at all; it is Turkey.

sets.title: Part 4 · Lecture: urban heat islands
sets.transcript:
L: This morning I'd like to explain the urban heat island effect - the reason cities are often several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside.
The main cause is surface materials. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight during the day and release the heat slowly at night, which is why the difference between city and countryside is often greatest after sunset.
A second cause is the lack of vegetation. Trees cool the air through shade and through evaporation of water from their leaves. Cities with fewer trees lose this natural cooling.
Third, heat is produced directly by human activity: vehicles, factories and, increasingly, air conditioners, which push hot air out of buildings.
The effects are serious. Heatwaves are more dangerous in cities, especially for elderly people, and higher temperatures increase electricity demand.
What can be done? One cheap solution is painting roofs white or light grey to reflect sunlight. Another is planting trees along streets; studies show that a tree-lined street can be up to five degrees cooler at midday. Some cities are also replacing car parks with small parks, and using permeable pavements that hold water and cool the surface as it evaporates.
In the next lecture, we'll look at how one city, Melbourne, has set a target of covering forty per cent of its area with tree canopy.

sets.title: Part 4 · Lecture: how memory works
sets.transcript:
L: Today we're going to look at how memory works, and what this means for studying.
Psychologists usually describe three stages. First, information enters sensory memory, which lasts less than a second. If we pay attention to it, it moves into working memory, which can hold only around four items at a time and fades within about twenty seconds unless we repeat it.
To keep information for longer, it has to be transferred into long-term memory. This happens best when we connect new information to something we already know - a process called elaboration.
One of the most reliable findings in memory research is the spacing effect. Studying the same material in several short sessions spread over days is far more effective than one long session the night before an exam.
Another powerful technique is retrieval practice, which simply means testing yourself. Trying to recall information, for example with flashcards, strengthens memory more than reading your notes again.
Sleep is also essential. During sleep, especially deep sleep, the brain replays and stabilises what we learned during the day.
Finally, a common myth: many students believe they have a fixed learning style, such as visual or auditory. Research has found little evidence that matching teaching to these styles improves results.

sets.title: Passage 1 · Farming upwards
sets.passage:
Farming upwards

Vertical farming is the practice of growing crops in stacked layers, usually indoors and under artificial light. Supporters describe it as a way to produce fresh food close to where people live, without the large areas of land that traditional agriculture needs. The idea is not new - the term was popularised by an American ecology professor in the late 1990s - but the falling price of LED lighting in the past fifteen years has turned it from a classroom thought experiment into a commercial industry.

Most vertical farms grow leafy greens such as lettuce, spinach and herbs. These plants are small, grow quickly and are sold at high prices per kilogram, which helps farms recover their considerable costs. Plants are usually grown without soil, either with their roots in a flowing nutrient solution, a method known as hydroponics, or suspended in air and sprayed with a fine mist, known as aeroponics. Because conditions are controlled, farms can harvest all year round and do not depend on the weather.

The environmental case for vertical farming rests largely on water and land. Operators claim to use up to ninety-five per cent less water than field farming, because water is recycled within a closed system rather than lost to evaporation and run-off. A single building can also produce the same quantity of lettuce as several hectares of open fields. In addition, since crops are grown in sealed rooms, pesticides are rarely needed.

Energy, however, is the industry's great weakness. Sunlight is free; artificial light is not. A farm must also run fans, pumps and air conditioning, and in hot climates cooling the rooms can use more power than the lights themselves. Several well-funded companies in Europe and North America closed between 2022 and 2024 when electricity prices rose sharply. Critics point out that if the electricity comes from coal, the carbon footprint of a vertical-farm lettuce may be higher than that of one grown in a field and transported a long distance.

For this reason, the most promising projects tend to be in places where land is scarce and expensive and where clean energy is available. Singapore, which imports more than ninety per cent of its food, has supported indoor farms as part of a national plan to produce a larger share of its nutritional needs locally by 2030. In Japan, some farms have been built inside former factories, reusing buildings that would otherwise stand empty.

It is unlikely that vertical farms will ever grow staple crops such as wheat or rice, which need large amounts of light and space and are sold cheaply. Instead, researchers expect the technology to remain a complement to conventional agriculture, supplying fresh, high-value produce to cities, and perhaps to remote communities and even, one day, to space stations.

sets.title: Passage 1 · The reef's night of spawning
sets.passage:
The reef's night of spawning

Once a year, usually a few nights after a full moon in late spring, many of the corals on Australia's Great Barrier Reef release their eggs and sperm into the water at almost the same moment. Divers who witness the event describe it as an upside-down snowstorm, as billions of small pink and white bundles drift towards the surface. Scientists first documented this mass spawning in 1981, when a group of young researchers from James Cook University noticed that dozens of coral species were spawning together.

The timing is remarkable because corals have no brain and no eyes. Researchers believe that several signals work together. Rising sea temperatures in spring prepare the corals to reproduce; the light of the moon, detected by light-sensitive proteins in the coral tissue, sets the night; and the darkness after sunset determines the hour. Spawning together greatly increases the chance that eggs and sperm from the same species will meet.

Once fertilised, the eggs develop into tiny larvae that float in the current for days or weeks. Only a very small proportion survive to settle on a hard surface, where each larva attaches itself and begins to grow into a new colony. This process is how reefs recover after damage from storms or heat.

In recent decades, recovery has become more difficult. Marine heatwaves cause bleaching, in which corals expel the algae that live inside them and give them most of their food and colour. If temperatures stay high for too long, the corals die. The Great Barrier Reef experienced mass bleaching in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024, giving damaged areas little time to recover between events.

Spawning has now become a tool for restoration. Teams collect bundles from the surface during spawning nights and raise larvae in floating pools or laboratory tanks, where many more survive than in the open sea. The larvae are then released onto damaged sections of reef. Some projects also breed corals that have survived heatwaves, hoping their offspring will be more heat-tolerant.

Scientists stress that these efforts cannot replace action on climate change. Restoration can help particular sites, but the reef covers an area larger than Italy. Without lower greenhouse gas emissions, they argue, heatwaves will continue to damage corals faster than any human programme can repair them.

sets.title: Passage 1 · The return of the night train
sets.passage:
The return of the night train

For much of the twentieth century, overnight trains were a normal way to travel across Europe. Passengers boarded in the evening, slept in a bunk and woke up in another country. From the 1990s, however, cheap flights and faster daytime trains made these services less popular, and many operators closed their sleeper routes because they were losing money.

In the last decade the trend has started to reverse. In 2016 the Austrian national railway took over several routes that German railways had abandoned and rebranded them under a single name. Within a few years, the company reported that most of its night services were full in summer, and it ordered new carriages with private compartments and small showers.

Several factors explain the revival. The most widely reported is concern about the climate impact of flying: a journey by electric train produces only a fraction of the carbon emissions of the same trip by plane. Night trains also save travellers the cost of a hotel, and they arrive in city centres rather than at airports far from town. Surveys suggest that younger travellers are particularly attracted by the idea of a slower, more memorable journey.

Running night trains is still difficult. Sleeping carriages carry far fewer passengers than seated ones, so ticket prices must be relatively high. Trains often pass through several countries, each with its own rules, fees and electrical systems, which adds cost and complexity. In addition, routes must be planned so that trains do not arrive too early in the morning, which limits the distances that can be covered.

Governments have begun to help. Some have reduced track access charges for overnight services, and the European Union has supported pilot routes. Even so, many experts believe that night trains will remain a small part of the travel market, suitable mainly for journeys of between 800 and 1,500 kilometres, where they compete most effectively with flying.

sets.title: Passage 1 · Seaweed on the menu
sets.passage:
Seaweed on the menu

Seaweed has been eaten for centuries in East Asia, where it appears in soups, salads and the wrapping of sushi. In recent years it has attracted interest far beyond this region, not only as food but also as a possible solution to several environmental problems.

Unlike most crops, seaweed needs no fresh water, no fertiliser and no land. It grows quickly in the sea, taking nutrients directly from the water around it. Some species can grow by up to half a metre in a single day under ideal conditions. Because it absorbs nitrogen and phosphorus, seaweed farming can help to clean coastal waters that have been polluted by run-off from agriculture.

Seaweed also absorbs carbon dioxide as it grows. This has led some companies to propose growing very large amounts of it and sinking it to the deep ocean, where the carbon would stay for hundreds of years. Scientists warn, however, that the real benefit is uncertain, because it is difficult to measure how much carbon would remain locked away and what effects large-scale sinking would have on ocean life.

As food, seaweed is rich in minerals such as iodine and calcium, and it contains protein and fibre. However, some types contain so much iodine that eating large quantities could be harmful, so health authorities in several countries recommend moderate consumption. Taste is another barrier: many consumers in Europe and North America find the flavour unfamiliar.

Today, more than 95 per cent of the world’s farmed seaweed is produced in Asia, with China and Indonesia the largest producers. Farms in Norway, Scotland and the United States are expanding, but they remain small. Experts say that new products, such as seaweed snacks and plant-based burgers containing seaweed, could help the industry grow outside Asia.

sets.title: Passage 1 · Learning from termites
sets.passage:
Learning from termites

In parts of Africa and Australia, termites build mounds that can rise more than five metres above the ground. Although the insects themselves are tiny and almost blind, their colonies construct structures that stay at a fairly stable temperature and humidity, even when the air outside changes greatly between day and night.

For many years scientists believed that the mounds worked like chimneys: warm air was thought to rise through a central shaft and escape at the top, pulling cooler air in at the bottom. More recent research, using sensors placed inside mounds, has shown that the process is more complex. The daily cycle of heating and cooling of the mound walls causes air to move in different directions at different times of day, slowly exchanging gases between the nest and the outside.

Architects have been inspired by these findings. The best-known example is a large office and shopping building in Harare, Zimbabwe, completed in the 1990s. Instead of conventional air conditioning, it uses fans, chimneys and thick concrete walls that store heat during the day and release it at night. According to its designer, the building uses about ten per cent of the energy of a similar building with full air conditioning.

Not everyone agrees that the building truly copies termites. Some biologists point out that it was designed according to the older chimney theory, which is now known to be incomplete. Nevertheless, they accept that the project helped to make the idea of "biomimicry" - learning from nature in design - popular among engineers.

Researchers are now studying whether the porous walls of termite mounds could inspire new building materials that "breathe", allowing air and moisture to pass through slowly. Such materials might reduce the need for mechanical ventilation in hot climates, although none has yet been used in a large building.

sets.title: Passage 2 · The lighthouse keepers
sets.passage:
The lighthouse keepers

A  For most of history, sailors approaching an unfamiliar coast at night had little more than luck to guide them. Reefs, sandbanks and headlands claimed thousands of ships, and as international trade grew in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, governments came under pressure from merchants and insurers to make their coasts safer.

B  The first warnings were simple fires lit on hills or towers. They were cheap but unreliable: rain could put them out, smoke could hide them, and from a distance one fire looked much like another, so a captain could not tell which harbour he was approaching.

C  Some of the most important lighthouses had to be built on isolated rocks, far from shore, where waves broke with tremendous force. Engineers developed interlocking granite blocks, shaped so that each stone was held by its neighbours, and towers were made wider at the base to resist the sea. Construction was possible only in calm summer weather and could take many years.

D  Once built, a lighthouse needed constant attention. Keepers trimmed wicks, polished the great lenses and wound the clockwork that turned the light, often staying awake through the night. A light that failed even for an hour could lead to disaster, and many keepers kept detailed logbooks recording every change in weather and every ship that passed.

E  On remote stations, keepers often lived with their wives and children. Supplies arrived by boat every few weeks, weather permitting, and children were taught at home or by correspondence. Many former keepers' children later remembered a childhood of freedom and responsibility, but also of isolation and long months without visitors.

F  From the 1960s onwards, automatic lights, electric lamps and satellite navigation gradually made keepers unnecessary. In Australia the last keepers left their stations in the 1990s. Today, many lighthouses have found new lives as museums, guesthouses and wedding venues, and volunteers maintain buildings that would otherwise decay.

sets.title: Passage 2 · Sleep and memory
sets.passage:
Sleep and memory

A  For centuries sleep was regarded as a passive state, a kind of switching off in which the body rested and the mind did nothing useful. Some philosophers even described it as a nightly rehearsal for death. Only in the twentieth century, with the invention of machines that record the electrical activity of the brain, did researchers discover how busy the sleeping brain really is.

B  Sleep is not uniform. During a typical night we pass through cycles of roughly ninety minutes, moving between light sleep, deep slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most vivid dreaming occurs. Evidence suggests that these stages support different kinds of learning: deep sleep appears especially important for facts and events, while REM sleep seems to help with skills and with linking new information to what we already know.

C  One of the most striking findings comes from experiments with rats that learned to run through a maze. Recording individual brain cells, scientists found that the same pattern of activity seen while the animals ran was repeated, at high speed, while they slept afterwards. Similar replay has since been observed in humans, and it is thought to transfer memories from short-term storage in a region called the hippocampus to longer-term storage in the cortex.

D  Sleep also influences how we remember emotional experiences. Studies suggest that REM sleep may preserve the content of an upsetting memory while reducing its emotional intensity, which could explain the common advice to "sleep on it" before making a difficult decision.

E  These findings have practical consequences. Students who stay up all night before an exam may remember less, not more, because they skip the sleep that would have stabilised the previous days' learning. In one experiment, students deprived of a night's sleep performed around forty per cent worse at forming new memories the following day.

F  Short daytime naps can also help. A nap of twenty to thirty minutes improves alertness, while a longer nap of about ninety minutes, which includes a full sleep cycle, has been linked to better performance on creative tasks. However, researchers warn that naps cannot fully replace a good night's sleep.

sets.title: Passage 2 · Green roofs
sets.passage:
Green roofs

A Covering roofs with soil and plants is not a new idea. Houses with grass roofs were built in Scandinavia more than a thousand years ago, where the thick layer of turf helped to keep heat inside during long winters.

B Modern green roofs are designed for a different purpose. As cities grow hotter, partly because concrete and asphalt absorb the sun’s heat, planners are looking for ways to cool buildings and streets. A planted roof can be up to 30 degrees cooler than a dark roof on a summer afternoon.

C A typical modern green roof has several layers: a waterproof membrane to protect the building, a drainage layer, a lightweight growing medium and, finally, the plants themselves. The drainage layer stores some rainwater for the plants and allows the rest to flow slowly away.

D Not all plants are suitable. Roofs are windy and dry, and the soil is usually shallow, so designers often use hardy succulents that store water in their leaves. Larger roofs with deeper soil can support grasses, small shrubs and even vegetables.

E Researchers have tried to calculate the advantages. Studies in several cities have found that green roofs reduce the energy needed for air conditioning in the floors directly below, slow the flow of stormwater into drains and provide habitats for insects and birds. The size of these benefits varies greatly depending on climate and design.

F Following early projects in Germany, cities such as Toronto, Copenhagen and Singapore now require or encourage green roofs on certain new buildings. Some offer tax reductions or grants to building owners who install them.

sets.title: Passage 2 · Clean water for rural schools
sets.passage:
Clean water for rural schools

A In many rural areas of the world, schools have no safe drinking water. Children who drink untreated water often suffer from stomach illnesses, which cause them to miss classes. Studies have linked poor water and sanitation to lower attendance, especially among girls.

B Previous efforts to solve the problem were not always successful. Some projects built expensive filtration systems that broke down after a few months because no one had been trained to repair them, and spare parts were not available locally.

C One organisation took a different approach. Instead of large machines, it gave schools simple ceramic filters, which remove most bacteria as water passes slowly through them. Each filter costs only a few dollars and can supply enough drinking water for a classroom for two years.

D The organisation also trained teachers and older pupils to clean the filters and to recognise when they needed replacing. Local potters were taught to produce the filters themselves, creating jobs and making replacements easy to obtain.

E Teachers now send a short text message each month reporting whether the filters are working. This allows the organisation to identify problems quickly and to send help only where it is needed, keeping costs low.

F However, filters alone cannot solve every problem. They do not remove chemical pollution, and they depend on schools having a regular supply of water to filter. In dry seasons, some schools still have to rely on water carried from distant rivers.

sets.title: Passage 2 · The science of the afternoon nap
sets.passage:
The science of the afternoon nap

A In a 1990s study, researchers testing pilots on long flights noticed something unexpected: pilots who were allowed a short planned rest in the cockpit made fewer mistakes later in the flight than those who stayed awake.

B Napping in the early afternoon is common in many cultures. In parts of southern Europe and Latin America, the traditional midday rest is linked to the hottest time of the day, but people everywhere tend to feel sleepy after lunch, even when they have not eaten a large meal.

C Scientists offer several explanations for this afternoon dip. One is that the body’s internal clock naturally produces a small drop in alertness about seven or eight hours after waking. Another is that the pressure to sleep builds up gradually during the day.

D A short nap of 10 to 20 minutes appears to improve alertness for up to three hours. Longer naps can lead to "sleep inertia", a feeling of grogginess that may last half an hour after waking, because the sleeper has entered a deeper stage of sleep.

E Some studies have found that people report feeling calmer and less irritable after a nap. However, these results depend on self-reports, which may be influenced by what participants expect to feel.

F Experts warn that frequent long naps can make it harder to fall asleep at night. They advise those who have trouble sleeping at night to avoid napping after mid-afternoon.

sets.title: Passage 3 · Bringing languages back
sets.passage:
Bringing languages back

Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that around forty per cent are endangered, meaning that children are no longer learning them as their first language. When the last fluent speakers die, a language can disappear within a single generation, taking with it songs, place names, ways of describing the natural world and much of a community's sense of identity.

Australia offers a stark example. Before European settlement, more than two hundred and fifty Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander languages were spoken across the continent. Government policies that separated children from their families and punished them for speaking their languages broke the chain of transmission. Today only around a dozen are still learned by children in the traditional way, although many more are being revived.

Revival is not a single method but a family of approaches. Where elderly speakers remain, communities may set up "master-apprentice" programmes, in which a younger learner spends hundreds of hours with a fluent elder, using only the language in everyday activities such as cooking, fishing or shopping. Where no speakers survive, revival depends on records: word lists made by missionaries, recordings collected by researchers and letters written by earlier generations.

The Kaurna language of the Adelaide Plains is often cited as a case of revival from written sources alone. The last known fluent speaker died in 1929, but two German missionaries had recorded about three thousand words and some grammar in the 1840s. Since the 1990s, community members and linguists have used these materials to rebuild the language, which is now taught in schools and heard in public ceremonies.

I would argue that the most important factor is not linguistic expertise but community control. Programmes designed by outsiders, however well-meaning, have often failed because they treated the language as an academic subject rather than as a living part of family and cultural life. Where communities decide which words to recreate, how the language should sound and who may teach it, revival tends to last.

Technology can help but should not be overestimated. Mobile apps and online dictionaries make languages visible and give young people a way to practise privately, which matters when they feel shy about making mistakes. Yet no app has yet produced a fluent speaker on its own. A language survives when people use it with each other: when parents speak it to their children and friends joke in it.

Critics sometimes ask whether it is worth spending public money on languages with only a few hundred learners. This, in my view, misunderstands the purpose. Research in Canada and Australia has linked language programmes to better school attendance and improved wellbeing among young Indigenous people. The value of a revived language cannot be measured only by the number of its speakers.

sets.title: Passage 3 · The gentle push
sets.passage:
The gentle push

Traditional economics assumed that people make choices rationally: they weigh costs and benefits, consider the future and act in their own best interests. Behavioural economics, which combines economics with psychology, challenges this picture. Its researchers have documented many ways in which real people depart from rational behaviour - they procrastinate, follow the crowd, and are strongly influenced by how choices are presented.

From these findings came the idea of the "nudge", popularised by the economist Richard Thaler and the legal scholar Cass Sunstein in a 2008 book. A nudge is any feature of the way a choice is presented that predictably changes behaviour without forbidding any option or significantly changing financial incentives. Putting fruit at eye level in a school canteen is a nudge; banning chips is not.

The best-known example concerns retirement savings. When workers must actively choose to join a pension scheme, many never get round to it. When they are enrolled automatically but can easily opt out, participation rises dramatically, often from around half to more than ninety per cent. Nobody is forced to save, yet far more people do.

Governments have embraced the approach. The United Kingdom set up a "Behavioural Insights Team" in 2010, and Australia, Singapore and many other countries followed. One widely reported trial found that adding a single sentence to tax reminder letters - telling recipients that most people in their town had already paid - increased payment rates. Such changes are attractive to officials because they are cheap and quick to test.

Nevertheless, nudging has its critics. Some argue that it is manipulative, because it works by exploiting mental shortcuts that people are not aware of. The psychologist Gerd Gigerenzer has suggested that, instead of steering citizens, governments should "boost" their abilities - for example, by teaching people how to understand risk statistics - so that they can make good decisions for themselves.

Others question the size of the effects. A review published in 2022 found that many nudges reported in early studies had much smaller effects when repeated on a larger scale, partly because successful results are more likely to be published than failures. Nudges may be useful for small, simple behaviours, these critics conclude, but they are no substitute for policies such as taxes or regulation when large problems like climate change are involved.

My own view is that the debate has sometimes been exaggerated on both sides. Every choice must be presented in some way; there is no neutral form or menu. The question is therefore not whether governments influence our decisions, but whether they do so openly, test what they do and allow us to choose differently.

sets.title: Passage 3 · Should cities ban cars from their centres?
sets.passage:
Should cities ban cars from their centres?

Over the past twenty years, a growing number of cities have closed parts of their centres to private cars. Oslo removed most on-street parking from its central area; Madrid restricted access for vehicles that do not meet emission standards; and many smaller towns have turned their main streets into pedestrian zones. Supporters argue that the results speak for themselves: cleaner air, fewer accidents and busier shops.

It is certainly true that air quality usually improves when traffic falls. Yet I believe the claim that businesses always benefit deserves more careful examination. Studies of pedestrian zones show mixed results. Cafés and clothes shops often do well, because people walking slowly are more likely to stop and browse. Businesses that sell heavy or bulky goods, such as furniture or hardware, may lose customers who cannot carry their purchases to a distant car park.

Equally important is the question of who is affected. Car-free centres are easiest to accept for people who live close by or have good public transport. For residents of outer suburbs, where buses may run only once an hour, losing the option of driving into the centre can mean losing access to jobs and services. In my view, any city that restricts cars without first improving public transport is simply moving the problem elsewhere.

There is also a risk that bans are introduced too quickly. Several cities have seen strong public protests when restrictions appeared without warning or consultation. By contrast, places that introduced changes gradually - starting with trial days, then weekends, then permanent closures - have generally found that opposition fades once residents experience the benefits.

None of this means that reducing car traffic is a mistake. The evidence that it saves lives and improves health is strong. But the most successful schemes are those that treat the car ban as one part of a wider plan, including better buses, safe cycle routes and delivery arrangements for businesses. A ban on its own is not a transport policy.

sets.title: Passage 3 · The value of boredom
sets.passage:
The value of boredom

Few people enjoy being bored. Faced with a queue, a delayed train or a dull meeting, most of us now reach immediately for a phone. Some psychologists argue that this habit may be costing us something valuable, because boredom, uncomfortable as it is, may encourage creative thinking.

In one frequently cited experiment, participants who first completed a deliberately tedious task - copying numbers from a telephone directory - later produced more ideas when asked to think of uses for a pair of plastic cups than participants who had not been bored. The researchers suggested that boredom pushes the mind to wander, and that mind-wandering helps people make unusual connections.

I find this explanation attractive, but the evidence is not as strong as popular articles often suggest. Several later studies have failed to repeat the original result, and many experiments use small groups of university students, who may not represent the wider population. It is also unclear whether a short burst of boredom in a laboratory resembles the long periods of boredom people experience in real life.

Moreover, boredom is not harmless for everyone. Research on prisoners, patients in hospital and workers in repetitive jobs links chronic boredom with stress, poor health and risky behaviour. To celebrate boredom as a source of creativity without recognising this darker side would, in my view, be irresponsible.

Perhaps the most useful lesson is a modest one. Occasional short periods without entertainment - a walk without headphones, a few minutes looking out of a window - may give the mind space to wander. Whether this makes us more creative remains an open question, but it is unlikely to do us harm.

sets.title: Passage 3 · Rewilding
sets.passage:
Rewilding

"Rewilding" is a term used for conservation projects that aim to restore natural processes rather than manage land in detail. Instead of planting trees in neat rows or removing every unwanted species, rewilding projects may reintroduce large animals, remove fences and allow rivers to flood naturally, then let nature take its course.

Supporters point to striking examples. When wolves were returned to a large national park in North America in the 1990s, they reduced the number of deer and changed their behaviour, allowing young trees to grow along rivers. In parts of Europe, beavers reintroduced after centuries of absence have built dams that slow floods and create wetlands for birds and insects.

I support many of these projects, but I am uneasy about how they are sometimes presented. There are also practical conflicts. Farmers living near rewilding areas may lose livestock to predators or crops to wild animals, and compensation schemes do not always cover their losses. If local people feel that decisions are imposed by distant organisations, projects are likely to face resistance. In my opinion, rewilding succeeds only when local communities share in the benefits, for example through tourism.

Finally, rewilding is not suitable everywhere. In small or crowded countries, there may simply not be enough space for large animals to roam. In such places, smaller projects - restoring a meadow, reconnecting a river to its floodplain - may achieve more than ambitious plans to reintroduce bears or lynx.
